title: The heartwood
hookLine: a man seeking heartwood who settles for twigs, bark or sapwood

lines: GREEN BRANCHES SMOKE AND GO OUT.
THE GOOD WOOD IS AT THE CENTER.
cards: Build a fire with green branches and you meet the problem fast: it smokes, it hisses, it goes out. The good wood is inside, the dense, dark center of an old tree that burns slow and lasts. Carpenters want it too.
It doesn't rot, it doesn't warp. But you can't get to it without cutting through everything else first, the leaves, the bark, the pale sapwood, and it's tempting to stop halfway.

teach.h: TWIGS AND LEAVES: GIFTS AND FAME
teach.b: The twenty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings was given, the text says, not long after Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, had split away from the community. The Buddha describes a man who needs heartwood.
He goes into the forest, finds a great tree, walks past the heartwood, the sapwood, the inner bark and the outer bark, and cuts off twigs and leaves. He carries them home thinking he's got heartwood.
A man with good eyes would say: he doesn't know what heartwood is, and his work won't get done. Then the Buddha maps the tree.
Someone goes forth out of faith and gains gifts, honor and fame; pleased with that, they look down on others. That's the twigs and leaves.
Someone else becomes truly virtuous, but stops, pleased with their virtue: the outer bark. Another reaches deep concentration, and stops there: inner bark.

Another reaches knowledge and vision, and stops: sapwood. Then the goal, plainly. This holy life is not for gifts and fame, not for virtue alone, not for concentration alone, not for knowledge and vision alone.
It's for the unshakable freedom of mind.
That is the heartwood. None of the outer layers is bad. Virtue is good; concentration is good; they're part of the same tree.
The mistake is only in stopping, pleased with yourself, and calling bark heartwood.

how: Buddhist teachers use the heartwood simile to remind monastics and lay practitioners that reputation, good conduct, concentration and insight are stages of the path, and that liberation of mind is its goal.

o: the oldest tree in a sacred forest
the hard core of a tree: the true goal
the soft inner bark used to make cloth

games.q: map the tree — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha says virtue and concentration are worthless
they're real layers of the same tree; the mistake is stopping there, pleased, and calling bark heartwood.
the text places this talk soon after Devadatta split away
MN 29 opens not long after Devadatta left the community.
the man in the story carries home sapwood
the first man walks past everything else and carries home twigs and leaves, thinking it's heartwood.

games.q: you went forth, and people now bring you gifts and praise your name. what does the Buddha's simile call that?
games.why: gifts, honor and fame are the twigs and leaves: the outermost part of the tree, the furthest from the heartwood.

practice: Pick one thing you care about, your work, your practice, a relationship, and sit with its layers: the twigs and leaves of praise and likes, the bark of good habits around it.
Then ask quietly what's at the center, the part that would still matter if nobody saw, and rest your attention there, as if your hand were on the grain of the wood.

wordCard.voice: The heartwood. Sara in Pali: the dense core of the tree, past the leaves, the bark and the sapwood. The unshakable freedom the path is for.

orig.note: Pali sara: heartwood, the core or essence. the discourse is the Mahasaropama Sutta, the greater simile of the heartwood.

carryVoice: Your line: take the heartwood. The applause is real, and still not the center. That's day four hundred twenty-six.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 29, Mahasaropama Sutta (the greater simile of the heartwood)
